The system maintains data gathered directly through questionnaires, surveys, interviews, and focus groups, as well as administrative records obtained from federal, state, local, and tribal criminal and civil justice agencies. Covered records pertain to both survey respondents and individuals tracked by justice agencies—such as crime victims, arrestees, defendants, inmates, and decedents in custody—and contain sensitive information including personal identifiers, criminal histories, immigration court proceedings, and medical or demographic data. Governed by strict federal privacy and confidentiality laws, including mandates under the Prison Rape Elimination Act and the Death in Custody Reporting Act, BJS may use this data solely for statistical and research purposes and is prohibited from using it for law enforcement, regulatory, or individual enforcement activities. The new system takes effect upon publication, while its routine uses will become effective on November 6, 2026, which is also the deadline for the public to submit comments electronically, by mail, or via email.

summary_responses.response: The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) has issued a notice inviting public and federal agency comments by December 7, 2026, on two revised information collections under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995. Under these rules, new wireless licensees must fund relocation reimbursements, timely-transition incentives, and aircraft radio altimeter retrofit rebates, all of which will be tracked, audited, and distributed by an independent Upper C-band Clearinghouse. The Upper C-band collection is estimated to involve 16,512 respondents at an annual cost of roughly $10.7 million, while the second, smaller collection listed in the notice covers 30 respondents regarding 3.7 GHz service licensee agreements and engineering analyses.

summary_responses.response: The Bureau of the Fiscal Service at the Department of the Treasury has issued a final rule amending the Uniform Offering Circular (31 CFR Part 356) to align its marketable securities auction regulations with planned auction system upgrades. The amendments clarify several technical definitions, eliminate outdated references such as paper bids and former CUSIP issuers, and replace specific web links with general website references to allow for greater administrative flexibility. To improve consistency between auction rules and public announcements, the rule also updates language to reflect current Treasury terminology regarding yields, discount rates, margins, and bid awards. Operationally, the rule modifies noncompetitive bidding requirements by mandating that submitters provide individual customer names and bid amounts—rather than summary totals—prior to the noncompetitive auction close to speed up post-auction processing. While the rule takes effect on October 15, 2026—with system-dependent provisions applying once the upgraded auction platform launches—it is exempt from standard notice-and-comment rulemaking procedures because Treasury securities relate to contracts.

summary_responses.response: Researchers from Tel Aviv University and Columbia University have introduced DiffTry (Differential Retries) to address how miscoordination in independently managed cloud microservices causes overloads, retry storms, and rejections of valuable transactions. Unlike traditional retry mechanisms that treat all traffic equally, DiffTry assigns different retry-attempt limits based on request priority, giving high-priority transactions more attempts to succeed during periods of overload while suppressing retry amplification. This lightweight, distributed, and stateless approach operates locally without requiring overload detection or cross-service coordination, remaining inactive under normal conditions while protecting critical traffic from both incidental spikes and malicious overload attacks. The authors develop an analytical framework for both single service pairs and complex microservice networks, establishing formal guarantees and an iterative method to quantify per-class rejection rates and prioritization. Simulations and a live Kubernetes deployment validate the model, demonstrating that DiffTry works as a drop-in service-mesh plugin requiring no application-code changes while achieving measured rejection rates that closely match theoretical predictions.

summary_responses.response: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has adopted a new airworthiness directive (AD), effective November 18, 2026, for certain Bombardier Model BD-700-2A12 airplanes. Prompted by an earlier Transport Canada directive, the rule addresses reports of low clearance between fuel, hydraulic, and support components in the right wing that could create a fuel tank ignition source during a lightning strike. To mitigate this unsafe condition, operators must replace specific clip-nuts and fuel tube assemblies, inspect the clearance between the hydraulic system and fuel vent tube, and replace hydraulic support brackets if low clearance is found. While five commenters supported the proposed rule, the FAA adopted the directive without substantive changes after addressing two other commenters who questioned why an emergency AD was not issued and requested reopening the comment period for additional reference and cost details. The FAA estimates the rule affects 60 U.S.-registered airplanes, costing $2,693 per aircraft for required actions and $5,772 for any necessary on-condition repairs, though manufacturer warranties may cover some or all of these expenses.

summary_responses.response: The Office of Personnel Management (OPM) has issued a direct final rule making technical revisions to its Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA) regulations to incorporate statutory amendments enacted in January 2021 and December 2023. These updates broaden the 12-month qualifying service requirement for title 5 FMLA eligibility—and consequently Paid Parental Leave—to include virtually all Federal civilian service, as well as honorable active military service in the Army, Navy, Air Force, Space Force, or Marine Corps. The rule also formally excludes Veterans Health Administration employees covered by a leave system under 38 U.S.C. 7421 from title 5 FMLA coverage, since they are governed by separate Department of Veterans Affairs provisions. Additionally, the document reflects statutory changes clarifying that annual and sick leave earned under authorities outside of title 5 may be substituted for unpaid FMLA leave, though no regulatory text revisions are necessary because existing rules already permit this. The rule will take effect on December 14, 2026, unless significant adverse comments are received by November 16, 2026, in which case OPM will withdraw the affected provisions and issue a notice of proposed rulemaking.
